questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Recreational activites in the area such as skiing, surfing, climbing, hiking etc. + academic opportunities in the form of subjects not available at UPCH

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy, UBC had held an information session before arrival and had sent all necessary information via email. The GoGlobal Office was very informative and helpful

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Information meeting and tour around campus

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: To get on campus housing, you entered a lottery with a 50% chance of receiving accomodation. Before the lottery, you made a prioritized list of where and how you wanted to live (number of roomates, area, price, cleanliness, etc). If selected, you were assigned an apartment/studio/room according to your wishes and availability. Campus has several different "areas" or clusters of accomodation which vary in terms of price, facilities, location, and type of students.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer:
I stayed in an apartment with 3 other students which had a normal kitchen with stove, oven, etc. You had to provide all cooking equipment and utensils yourself including pots, pans, plates, etc. 
Meal plans were also available but I did not use them.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about on campus housing? *
questions.answer: UBC is located quite separately from the rest of Vancouver (and the infrastructure in Vancouver with regard to traffic is not great) so on campus housing is great/recommended unless you want to commute for quite a long time every day. The probability of getting a room is quite high when you are an exchange student and on campus housing is both cheap and a great way to meet other students.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Figuring out *how* to apply for courses is really confusing when you wish to take graduate courses. You are told one thing (officially) but the experience of other students and reality are quite another thing. It is really stressful and confusing since the process varies for different faculties, courses, professors, etc. For starters, UBC does not *officially* allow exchange students in their political science programme, but they do if you get lucky and ask the professors of the courses for permission to enroll anyway. Second, you have to fill out all kinds of documents regarding course registration for undergraduate courses - even though you don't want to enroll in undergraduate courses.

However, once you have figured out how to do it, getting enrolled is actually pretty easy and a smooth process.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: To be enrolled in graduate courses, you have to ask each professor individually for permission to take their course and sign a document provided by GoGlobal. You do this either by email before you arrive (HIGHLY recommended) or in-person once you arrive. If permitted, you need to get the administration of the faculty to enroll you (fairly easy, just sent them an email). Although UBC does not officially allow exchange students in their graduate programme, I found that it was possible to get graduate courses anyway. However, I greatly recommend taking courses at the School of Public Policy and Global Affairs (PPGA) as well.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The GoGlobal office was available, both via email and in-person, but they could not really help since you kind of had to do the process yourself and through a different way than the official process. I found that the best help was to ask former KU students for help.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got 2 courses that were my first priority and 1 that was my second priority

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Graduate courses are difficult to register for but worth it in my opinion. However, you have to register in a very unstructured, non-official way (see above). Ask former KU students for help and begin in good time by emailing the professors whose courses you want to take. Also: it will all work out in the end, even though it is a chaotic process.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
I found the level to be a bit lower at UBC than UPCH, meaning that getting good grades requires a lower - or at least different kind of - effort than at home. For graduate courses, you have to put in more effort on a week-to-week basis than back home because you are expected (required in some courses) to participate orally every week. You also have to hand in several assignments during the term and/or do presentations that account for part of your grade. On the one hand, this means that you have to put in (more) effort each week. However, this also means that your final exam or assignment does not decide everything. The amount of reading is generally lower than at UPCH but the amount of required assignments and written hands-in are definetely higher.

If you are the type of student that does your readings and work every week, then the required effort is probably lower than at UPCH, but if you are the type that does all the readings in the final week of the semester, then the required effort might feel higher at UBC as you are forced to do at least a bit every week.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The style of teaching varies greatly from professor to professor. At the School of Public Policy and Global Affairs (PPGA), seminars were 3 hours once a week and resembled a mixture of lectures, discussion and exercises, fairly similar to UPCH but with much smaller classes (5-15) and higher expectations for student participation. 
At my Political Science course, the seminar was also 3 hours once a week but teaching was entirely student-based discussion with no lecture or introduction from the professor. However, I think that was quite unique for the course and not representative of all political science courses.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Policy Dimensions of Energy Systems
Global environmental politics
Global governance

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Courses at the School of Public Policy and Global Affairs (PPGA) are really great if you want more policy and practically oriented courses. They are less "academic" and more "practical" in the sense that you learn less theory and frameworks and read less academic articles. Instead, you read texts from policy institutes, think tanks, and governments, engage more in actual empirical cases and practice skills such as international negotation, writing policy briefs, and oral debates.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: The cost of living in Vancouver is fairly high, so going grocery shopping for food items such as vegetables and dairy products are more expensive than in DK. Going out for dinner/movies/activites are generally a bit cheaper than Copenhagen but not a lot

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
UBC has a club for EVERYTHING, so no matter what your interests are, you can find like-minded people to hang out with. However, since the campus is so huge, it is rare that the univeristy as such hosts anything in itself. Instead, events are hosted by individual communities, faculties, and clubs.
Apart from clubs, UBC has its own farm, forest, beaches and several museums on campus.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Join the Varsity Outdoor Club (VOC) if you like outdoor activities such as hiking, ski touring, climbing, and kayaking. The club plans tours almost every weekend which are open to join and only costs transportation and evt. gear rental. If you are a member, you can also rent all gear for free + it is a great place to meet really cool people.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Get outside Vancouver and explore the amazing nature that British Columbia has to offer. Within only a couple of hours of driving, you can do almost anything outdoorsy. Go climbing in Squamish, ski in Whistler, hike in Garabaldi, kayak around the Gulf Islands, surf on Vancouver Island, and bike along the Sunshine Coast. You can almost always find a tour to join with the VOC (see above)

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Super easy! People in Vancouver are extremely friendly, open and easy to talk to

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join some of the clubs and sports teams and talk to the people in your courses. It is super easy to get caught in the exchange "bubble" where you only talk to other exchange students who are also looking for friends, but getting to know some local students is really great! Canadians are super friendly so just ask someone to have a cup of coffee or watch a hockey game on campus.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: You have to adjust to the fact that people actually talk to strangers in Canada (as opposed to Copenhagen), but that is a great thing once you learn that you don't have to tell your entire life story every time someone asks "How are you?".

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Everyone is really open, friendly, polite and hospitable! In addition, the city of Vancouver is very ethnically diverse meaning that you can meet people from literally all over the world.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Join as many clubs as possible, especially the VOC
Go enjoy the nature outside the city every time you can
Get housing on campus or at least nearby, unless you are willing to commute for a long time every day

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: The semester is pretty short at UBC so if you can, plan to stay for some time after you are done. That will allow you to explore more of B.C. and hang out with some of the cool people you have met

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting to meet cool people, enjoy the AMAZING outdoor experiences in BC, and having more practically oriented courses

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: (some) Graduate courses require a decent amount of preparation each week but are, in my opinion, definetely worth it

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
